:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=-2x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-4x
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-4 \, \textrm{d}u=16x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt {\ln 4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-2\ln 4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}16x{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\cdot 16x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-4({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-4(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\  & =4\left(\frac{15}{16}\right) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}5x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}5{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}5{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(2) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=2{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2\operatorname{ln}⁡5$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}}\frac{1}{5}x{e}^{2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}}{e}^{2{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{20}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{20}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}(25-1) \\  & =\frac{24}{20} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}x{4}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{{4}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(4-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}2x\cdot {3}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\cdot {3}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\,|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}({3}^{1}-{3}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}x{e}^{3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}x=
$$
{{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $4\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}x{e}^{3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(16-2) \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\frac{12{e}^{x}}{3{e}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x=
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{e}^{x}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $7$ | $16$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\frac{12{e}^{x}}{3{e}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\frac{4}{3{e}^{x}+1}\cdot 3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{7}^{16}\frac{4}{u}\cdot \,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{7}^{16}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{7}^{16} \\  & =4(\operatorname{ln}⁡(16)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{16}{7}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $3\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}2x{e}^{3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}{e}^{3{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({3}^{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}x\,⟹\,\frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}{3}$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}}x{e}^{{x}^{2}/3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}}{e}^{{x}^{2}/3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡8)/3}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡8)/3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡8)/3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({e}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡8)/3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\sqrt[3]{8}-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(2-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^3+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac 1 3 \textrm{d}u = x^2 \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot \,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u = e^{2x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u = e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{e}^{2x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that $e^{2x} + 1 > 0$ for all $x.$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=-2x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-4x
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-4 \, \textrm{d}u=16x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt {\ln 4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-2\ln 4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}16x{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\cdot 16x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-4({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-4(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\  & =4\left(\frac{15}{16}\right) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we want to calculate $$
\displaystyle \int 2x e^{x^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then both $u$ and its derivative $u'=2x$ appear in the integrand:

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} e^{\overbrace{x^2}^u}\,\textrm d x
$$

Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

Let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.
$$

We now substitute our expressions into the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\underbrace{2x\,\text{d}x}_{\text{d}u} \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^3+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac 1 3 \textrm{d}u = x^2 \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot \,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u = e^{2x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u = e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{e}^{2x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that $e^{2x} + 1 > 0$ for all $x.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's evaluate the following definite integral:

$$
\displaystyle{\int_{0}^{3} xe^{x^{2}}\, \textrm{d}x}
$$

We'll use the change of variable method, which comprises three steps:

**Step1:**  Change of variable in the integrand.

Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = 2x 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u = x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

**Step 2:** Find the new limits of integration.

We create a table below to change our limits of integration from $x$ to $u{:}$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $9$ |

**Step 3:** Evaluate the integral in the new variable $u.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{9}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{9}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{9}-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+1.$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline x & -1 & 0 \\ \hline u & 2 & 1 \\ \hline\end{array}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^0 x(x^2+1)^3\,\textrm{d}x=\int_2^1 u^3\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}{|}_{2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{1}^{4}-{2}^{4}}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1-16}{4} \\  & =-\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Important**: Note that in this example, when we changed the limits the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 \ldots \textrm{d}x
$$ became $$
\displaystyle \int_{2}^1 \ldots \textrm{d}u.
$$ When changing the limits, it is important to respect the order in which the limits are applied. The lower limit of the integral in $u$ must correspond to the lower limit of the integral in $x.$ Same for the upper limit.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{3}+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & ={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^3+2.$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline x & -1 & 2 \\ \hline u & 1 & 10 \\ \hline\end{array}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^2 \dfrac{1}{(x^3+2)}\,x^2\textrm{d}x=\int_1^{10} \dfrac{1}{u}\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10).\end{aligned}
$$
